title: Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the element whose absolute difference from a given key is smallest. If two elements are equally close, return the smaller one. Explain how binary search plus a comparison of the two neighbours around the closing window finds it.
shortTitle: Minimum Difference Element (Closest Element to a Key in a Sorted Array)

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Difference Element is a Modified Binary Search problem. We binary-search for the key, and if we find it exactly the difference is zero. If we do not find it, the closing window leaves the start pointer just above the key and the end pointer just below it, so the closest element is whichever of those two neighbours has the smaller absolute difference, with ties broken toward the smaller value.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, foreign-exchange desk quotes are stored as a sorted array, and when Rajesh wants to convert at a target rate that may not be quoted exactly, we must offer the nearest available quote. We binary-search the quotes, and if the exact rate is missing we compare the two quotes bracketing it and offer the closer one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search; if the key is absent the start and end pointers straddle it, so return whichever neighbour is closer, preferring the smaller on a tie.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Difference Element is a Modified Binary Search problem. We binary-search for the key, and if we find it exactly the difference is zero. If we do not find it, the closing window leaves the start pointer just above the key and the end pointer just below it, so the closest element is whichever of those two neighbours has the smaller absolute difference, with ties broken toward the smaller value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, foreign-exchange desk quotes are stored as a sorted array, and when Rajesh wants to convert at a target rate that may not be quoted exactly, we must offer the nearest available quote. We binary-search the quotes, and if the exact rate is missing we compare the two quotes bracketing it and offer the closer one.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search; if the key is absent the start and end pointers straddle it, so return whichever neighbour is closer, preferring the smaller on a tie.

sections.s2_technical:
We binary-search with `start = 0` and `end = n - 1`. If `arr[mid] == key` we return `arr[mid]` immediately, difference zero. The standard moves apply otherwise: `key < arr[mid]` sets `end = mid - 1`, `key > arr[mid]` sets `start = mid + 1`. When the loop ends with `start > end`, the key lies between `arr[end]` and `arr[start]`, so we compare `arr[start] - key` against `key - arr[end]` and return the element with the smaller difference. For example, `if (arr[start] - key < key - arr[end]) return arr[start]; else return arr[end];`.

The reason this works is that binary search, when it fails to find the key, always leaves `start` pointing at the smallest element greater than the key and `end` pointing at the largest element smaller than the key, which are exactly the two candidates for the closest element. Using the less-than comparison in that final check means a tie returns `arr[end]`, the smaller value, satisfying the tie-break rule.

A senior nuance is guarding the edges: if the key is smaller than every element, `end` becomes minus one and we return `arr[0]`; if the key is larger than every element, `start` becomes `n` and we return the last element. Those edge guards are easy to forget. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores foreign-exchange quotes in a sorted array, and when Rajesh requests conversion at a target rate that may not be quoted, the desk must offer the nearest available quote. This is exactly how Minimum Difference Element works: find the element closest to the key.

Problem 2 — Scanning all quotes to find the closest is wasteful when there are many quotes. This is why we binary-search and, on a miss, compare only the two quotes straddling the target, preferring the smaller rate on a tie so the customer is never over-charged by rounding.

The code defines a `FxQuoteService` exposing `closestQuote(quotes, target)` returning the nearest quote. A `Demo` finds the nearest quote for a target rate and logs it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: quotes 82, 84, 87, 91, 95 and target 89.

Step 1: 89 is within range, so we enter the search. start is 0, end is 4, mid is 2, quote at 2 is 87, and 89 is greater so start becomes 3.

Step 2: start is 3, end is 4, mid is 3, quote at 3 is 91, and 89 is less so end becomes 2.

Step 3: loop ends with start 3 and end 2. Quote at start is 91 with difference 2; quote at end is 87 with difference 2. The differences tie, and the less-than comparison is false, so we return quote at end, 87, the smaller value.


sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Difference Element is a Modified Binary Search problem where I find the array element whose absolute difference from the key is smallest. I binary-search for the key, and if I hit it exactly the difference is zero and I am done. The real insight is what happens when the search fails: the loop always finishes with the start pointer sitting on the smallest element greater than the key and the end pointer on the largest element smaller than the key, so those two neighbours straddle the key and one of them must be the closest.

So on a miss I simply compare the difference between the upper neighbour and the key against the difference between the key and the lower neighbour, and return whichever is smaller. I write that comparison with a strict less-than so that a tie returns the lower neighbour, which satisfies the rule of preferring the smaller value. I also guard the two edges first: if the key is below everything I return the first element, and if it is above everything I return the last.

At the National Bank of India I used this on the foreign-exchange desk, where quotes are stored sorted and a customer like Rajesh may ask to convert at a target rate that is not quoted exactly. I binary-searched the quotes and, when the exact rate was missing, compared only the two quotes straddling the target and offered the closer one, preferring the smaller rate on a tie so rounding never worked against the customer. Explaining the straddle invariant and the tie-break is what shows an interviewer I understand why only two candidates ever need checking.
